Rent Garments
rent GAR-ments
noun
Rent is the old past tense and participle of rend (Saxon hrendan, to tear), and garment comes through Old French garnement, “equipment, clothing,” from garnir, to furnish. The phrase names clothing torn deliberately as a public sign.

Biblical Definition

Rent garments are torn clothes — the ancient, public, bodily sign of grief, horror, or protest. Jacob rends first: told his son is dead, “Jacob rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days” (Gen 37:34), and Reuben had already rent his at the empty pit (Gen 37:29). Job rends his mantle and worships in the same motion (Job 1:20). Josiah rends his clothes when the book of the law is read (2Ki 22:11), and that tearing is the beginning of a reformation. Barnabas and Paul rend theirs when Lystra would sacrifice to them (Act 14:14), for the sign serves horror at blasphemy as readily as sorrow at death. There the danger begins. The high priest was forbidden it: “he that is the high priest among his brethren…shall not uncover his head, nor rend his clothes” (Lev 21:10). Yet at the trial of Christ, “the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy” (Mat 26:65) — Caiaphas breaking the law of his own office to condemn the Lord of it, the torn robe declaring that this priesthood was finished before ever the veil was rent. Against all outward tearing stands Joel: “rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God” (Joe 2:13). Cloth is cheap; hearts are not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Clothing deliberately torn as a public sign of grief, horror at blasphemy, or contrition.

expand to see more

RENT, torn; parted by violence: the old participle of rend.

GARMENT, any article of clothing, as a coat, a gown, or a mantle.

To rend the garments was the eastern sign of mourning and of horror.

The high priest was expressly forbidden to rend his clothes (Lev 21:10).

Joel commands the inward tearing instead: rend your heart (Joe 2:13).

Key Scripture

Gen 37:34 — "And Jacob rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days."

Job 1:20 — "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped,"

Mat 26:65 — "Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy; what further need have we of witnesses? behold, now ye have heard his blasphemy."

Joe 2:13 — "And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil."

Modern Corruption

The perennial temptation is the torn coat without the torn heart — grief performed for an audience while the soul is untouched.

expand to see more

The corruption of this sign is as old as the sign itself, and Joel names it: garments rent while hearts stay whole. Every age finds its own cloth to tear. Ours has made public lamentation a currency — the statement issued, the ribbon worn, the sorrow displayed before witnesses and audited by them — and the display can be total while repentance is nil. Christ marked the same instinct in men who disfigured their faces that they might appear unto men to fast (Mat 6:16). The sign is not the sin; Jacob and Job and Josiah rent honestly, and God did not despise it. The sin is the substitution: making the visible token do the work of the invisible turning, so that a man mourns for a whole nation’s wickedness and never once mourns for his own.

The high priest’s torn robe is the sharpest word here. Aaron’s successor was forbidden to rend his garments precisely because his office signified an unbroken priesthood; the anointing on his head made his very clothing holy. When Caiaphas tore his robe to charge the Son of God with blasphemy, he condemned himself twice — breaking the law of his office and calling the truth a blasphemy in the same breath — and, unwittingly, he preached. That torn robe announced the end of the Aaronic line, and within hours the veil was rent from the top to the bottom by a hand that was not a man’s (Mat 27:51). One tearing opened the way in; one tearing shut the old order out. The gospel calls not for cloth but for what Joel commanded: rend your heart, and turn unto the LORD your God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Torn clothing as the AV sign of mourning, horror, and contrition — and Joel’s rebuke of it.

expand to see more

Rent — old past participle of rend, Saxon hrendan, “to tear.”

Jacob, Reuben, Job, and Josiah all rend their clothes in grief (Gen 37:29, 34; Job 1:20; 2Ki 22:11).

Apostles rend theirs in horror at attempted idolatry (Act 14:14).

The high priest was forbidden the sign (Lev 21:10); Caiaphas used it anyway (Mat 26:65).

Joel’s crown: rend your heart, and not your garments (Joe 2:13).

Usage

"He rent his clothes and put on sackcloth: the eastern grammar of grief."

"The high priest rent his clothes — the law of his own office broken to condemn its Fulfiller."

"Rend your heart, and not your garments: the only tearing God requires."
